comment: Ratcheting waivers for the schemathesis contract-fuzzing legs (M-T9.21). A rule names one ROOT CAUSE — a check plus a regex over the operation label — and points at the entry in docs/audits/schemathesis-findings-2026-08.md that explains it with a repro. The ratchet bites both ways: a finding no rule matches FAILS the run (a new bug, or a known one spreading to a surface no rule claimed), and a rule that matches nothing across the whole run ALSO fails it (fix the root cause, delete the rule and strike the register entry in the same PR). Rules are deliberately NOT machine-generated: an unexplained waiver is indistinguishable from a silent skip. `kind` is `bug` (a defect we are choosing not to fix in the discovery PR) or `by-design` (the check disagrees with a deliberate decision). STALE IS NOT FIXED: a rule that matches nothing is the ratchet asking a QUESTION — did the root cause go away, or did the fuzzer stop reaching it? Answer it against the emitter before deleting the rule. W10 spent three nights failing the run as "stale" while `errorStatuses("workflow")` still had no 404 arm; the case had simply stopped being generated when the spec shape shifted (the seed is pinned, but the cases are derived FROM the spec, and a data-dependent finding needs a row an earlier case created). A finding whose reproduction depends on run data carries `intermittent` for exactly that reason — W10 was one and did not say so.
backendsComment: `backends` names the LEGS a rule claims, and drives BOTH halves of the ratchet: a rule only absorbs a finding on a leg it claims (so a known root cause spreading to a sixth surface is still unwaived), and it is only judged stale on a leg it claims (so fixing it on python means dropping "python" from the list in the same PR, while the rule survives for the legs that still reproduce it). Each leg is its own process against its own database, so staleness cannot be pooled across them. Omitting `backends` means all five. The elixir leg carries NO rules yet: its toolchain could not be run locally when the matrix landed, so it runs as a discovery cell (continue-on-error in schemathesis.yml) until a nightly run seeds its rules — see the audit's "elixir leg" section.

waivers.reason: F9 — schemathesis counts an unknown QUERY parameter as a schema-violating request that the API accepted. Ignoring unrecognised query parameters is ordinary HTTP behaviour and deliberate here; recorded so the decision is visible rather than silently filtered out of the check set. Reproduces identically on every booted backend, which is the evidence that it is the DECISION and not one backend's router.

waivers.intermittentReason: Reaching the overflow needs TWO independent things in one run: an out-of-int32 `qty` (the declared `{type: integer}` permits it) AND a path `{id}` that resolves to a row the fuzzer created earlier — a random uuid 404s before the column is ever written. So its absence from a given run is not evidence of a fix; it reproduced on the discovery run and not on the next. Removing this exemption means pinning it as a deterministic case in the behavioral tier — the shape W6's fix took (#2615).
waivers.reason: F11 — an `int` body field publishes `{"type":"integer"}` with NO bound and validates as `z.number().int()` with no bound, while the column behind it is Postgres `int4`: a value the published contract permits (9543751572142) overflows and 500s. Same declared-vs-enforced family as F7, one level down — F7 was the declared type, this is the missing declared range. Scoped to the one operation it reproduces on deliberately: widening it is a decision, not a default. Uncovered when the over-broad W1 (`^POST /api/`) was deleted with F1's fix.

waivers.intermittentReason: The consequence half of W11 inherits its data dependency exactly: no overflow in a run means no 500, and no 500 means nothing for status_code_conformance to report. Exempt from the staleness ratchet for the same reason, and it graduates with W11.
waivers.reason: The consequence half of W11: a 500 is not a declared response on any route, so F11's overflow also trips status_code_conformance. Clears with W11 when `int` gets its declared int32 range on all five backends.

F16 — a create whose `X id` reference is a WELL-FORMED uuid for a row that does not exist reaches Postgres and trips the foreign key: asyncpg raises ForeignKeyViolationError, SQLAlchemy re-raises it as IntegrityError, and nothing between the repository and the router maps it, so it surfaces as 500. F2's successor: F2 was the MALFORMED reference (fixed on all five in #2555 by publishing + enforcing `format: uuid`), this is the well-formed one, which no amount of wire validation can catch — it needs the existence check the domain layer already knows how to express. Scoped to the two creates in these fixtures that carry a cross-aggregate reference.
The consequence half of W20: 500 is not a declared response on any route, so F16's foreign-key escape also trips status_code_conformance. Clears with W20.

F17 — F7 (declared `type` not honoured: the wire validators coerce) is still OPEN on python. `Money.amount` publishes `{"type":"number","minimum":0}`, and a JSON boolean is accepted for it: pydantic's lax mode treats `false` as `0.0` (bool is an int subclass in Python), so the create answers 201 for a body the published contract rejects. F7's fix landed on the Hono emitter only (2026-08-16) — the node leg is clean here and python is not, which is precisely the per-backend divergence this matrix exists to surface.

F20 — a NUL character inside a declared `string` reaches Postgres, which rejects it with `CharacterNotInRepertoireError (22021)`, and the driver's error escapes as a 500. NUL is a legal JSON string character and an illegal Postgres `text` byte, so nothing on the write path refuses it. NARROWED 2026-09-03: this rule also carried F19 (a declared `date-time` the wire layer did not parse reaching `DateTime.Parse` in the domain). F19 is FIXED on .NET — measured on a booted app, `placedAt: ""` and `placedAt: "not-a-date"` both answer 422 through the WireFormatException arm (M-T6.48), not 500 — so the rule now claims only the NUL half. That half reproduces on java too and is a storage-layer refusal rather than a parse, which is why it is its own slice.

The consequence half of W24: 500 is not a declared response on any route, so F20's NUL escape also trips status_code_conformance. Clears with W24. Narrowed with it on 2026-09-03 — F19 no longer reproduces on .NET.

F22 — a bodyless operation POST answers 415 before the path parameter is looked at. ASP.NET's media-type check fires before model binding, so a request with a malformed `{id}` AND no body is answered by the one thing the contract says least about; 415 is not in the set of statuses the fuzzer counts as a rejection. The honest answer is the declared 422 for the unparseable identifier. PATTERN WIDENED 2026-09-01: it was written from the two `orders` routes of the discovery run and matched only those, so the SAME finding on `POST /api/customers/{id}/update` and `POST /api/wallets/{id}/freeze` arrived unwaived on a later run. Measured on a booted app, the 415 does not depend on the id being malformed at all — a VALID uuid with no Content-Type answers 415 too — so the shape is every operation POST, which is what the pattern now says. node, python and java are clean on this check, so the 415 is a .NET-only divergence rather than a shared decision.

waivers.intermittentReason: Whether the empty-string create is REACHED depends on whether the same generated body also carries the NUL byte of F20, which 500s first and is itself data-dependent — two runs of the same pinned seed produced the write half on one and only the read half (W28) on the other. Absence is therefore not evidence of a fix; it graduates with F21.
waivers.reason: F21's WRITE half, RE-DIAGNOSED (2026-09-03) — the original reason said `name` publishes `minLength: 1` in the request schema and .NET enforces it in neither. Measured on a booted app, both halves of that are wrong: `CreateCustomerRequest` publishes NO length bound at all (the request DTO already carries `AllowEmptyStrings = true`), and the bound the model DOES declare (`invariant email.length > 0`) IS enforced — `{"name":"n","email":""}` answers 422 with `pointer: /email` from FluentValidation. `{"name":"","email":"x"}` answering 201 is CORRECT: `name` carries no invariant. So whatever this rule is absorbing on `POST /api/customers`, it is not an unenforced `minLength`. The READ half (W28) was a real contract violation and is FIXED; this rule stays only because the leg cannot be run here to say what it is now catching, and retiring a rule on a guess is how W31 came back. Re-triage against a nightly before touching it.

waivers.intermittentReason: The finding needs the fuzzer to generate a MALFORMED query chunk (a parameter with an empty name, `?=%C3%A0`) against a read route. It did so ×4 on run 33382822525 and ×0 on the two runs before it — the same low rate that made W31 look permanently stale and got it wrongly retired (see F24). Declared intermittent so the staleness half cannot ask that question again on two samples.
waivers.reason: F28 — java answers 400 for an UNPARSEABLE query string and no read route declares a 400. Replaces W32 (F25), which is FIXED: the paged `page`/`pageSize` bounds now answer the declared 422, matching the other four backends and java's own published set. What is left is narrower and java-only: Tomcat refuses to parse a malformed chunk and throws before any handler runs, so the request never reaches the wire-validation tier that would make it a 422. The other four backends IGNORE the junk parameter and answer 200 (the deliberate decision W8 records), and Tomcat 11 exposes no leniency knob — no `parameterParsing*` attribute on Connector or Parameters — so java cannot join them by configuration. 400 is therefore the honest answer, and declaring it on the SHARED read contract would publish a status the other four never produce. Clearing this means either a container-level parser change or a java-only declaration; neither is a fuzzer fix.

F21 on java, RE-DIAGNOSED (2026-09-03) — the original reason said `name` publishes `minLength: 1` and the create accepts `""` with 201, "exactly as on .NET". Measured on a booted Spring app: java publishes NO `minLength` anywhere — not on `CreateCustomerRequest`, not on `CustomerResponse` — so there is no published bound to go unenforced, and the bound the model does declare is enforced (`email: ""` answers 422 from the domain invariant). `name: ""` answering 201 is correct. Java under-publishes where .NET used to over-publish; neither is what this rule's text claimed. Kept, un-retired, for the same reason as W27: the leg is what has to say what it catches.
